function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

I’m not able to run shell commands or push to a remote repository from here, but I can walk you through the exact steps you’d need to take on your own machine (or CI environment) and give you ready‑to‑paste snippets for the Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests and GitHub Actions workflow.  

Below is a **step‑by‑step guide** that you can copy into a terminal or a script.  
Feel free to adjust paths, image names or other details to match your own conventions.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
# 1. Clone the repo
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> **Tip:** If you’re cloning over HTTPS instead of SSH, replace the URL with  
> `https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git`.

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the repo & generate artefacts

### 2.1 Inspect the repo

```bash
# 2.1 Quick inspection – list files, check package.json, etc.
tree -L 2
cat package.json
```

> Look for:
> * `main` entry in `package.json` (e.g., `"main": "index.js"`)
> * Any `scripts.start` entry (e.g., `"start": "node index.js"`)
> * Port the app listens on (often `process.env.PORT || 3000`)

### 2.2 Create a Dockerfile

You can use the helper tool to generate a basic Dockerfile.  
If you prefer to write it manually, see the snippet below.

```bash
# 2.2 Generate Dockerfile via the provided tool
functions.create_a_docker_file({
  directory_name: ".",
  base_image: "python:3.10-slim",   # <-- choose the base image you want
  maintainer: "Your Name <you@example.com>",
  expose_port: 3000,                # <-- adjust to your app’s port
  entrypoint: "node index.js"       # <-- adjust to your start command
})
```

> **Manual Dockerfile (recommended for Node.js)**  
> ```dockerfile
> # 2.2 Dockerfile – nodejs-welcome
> FROM node:18-alpine
> 
> # Set working directory
> WORKDIR /app
> 
> # Copy package files first to leverage Docker cache
> COPY package*.json ./
> 
> # Install dependencies
> RUN npm ci --only=production
> 
> # Copy source code
> COPY . .
> 
> # Expose the port your app listens on
> EXPOSE 3000
> 
> # Default command
> CMD ["node", "index.js"]
> ```
> Save this as `Dockerfile` in the repo root.

### 2.3 Generate Kubernetes YAMLs

```bash
# 2.3 Generate Kubernetes YAML via the provided tool
functions.create_kubernetes_yaml_file({
  directory_name: ".",
  deployment_name: "nodejs-welcome-deployment",
  image_name: "zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest",
  replicas: 3,
  port: 3000,
  service_type: "ClusterIP"
})
```

> **Manual Kubernetes manifests (recommended)**  
> ```yaml
> # 2.3 deployment.yaml
> apiVersion: apps/v1
> kind: Deployment
> metadata:
>   name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
> spec:
>   replicas: 3
>   selector:
>     matchLabels:
>       app: nodejs-welcome
>   template:
>     metadata:
>       labels:
>         app: nodejs-welcome
>     spec:
>       containers:
>         - name: nodejs-welcome
>           image: zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest
>           ports:
>             - containerPort: 3000
>           env:
>             - name: PORT
>               value: "3000"
> ```
> ```yaml
> # 2.3 service.yaml
> apiVersion: v1
> kind: Service
> metadata:
>   name: nodejs-welcome-service
> spec:
>   type: ClusterIP
>   selector:
>     app: nodejs-welcome
>   ports:
>     - protocol: TCP
>       port: 3000
>       targetPort: 3000
> ```

### 2.4 Create a GitHub Actions workflow

```bash
# 2.4 Create .github/workflows/build.yml
mkdir -p .github/workflows
cat > .github/workflows/build.yml <<'EOF'
name: Build & Push Docker Image

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      - name: Checkout code
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up Docker Buildx
        uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

      - name: Log in to Docker Hub
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          username: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}
          password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }}

      - name: Cache Docker layers
        uses: actions/cache@v4
        with:
          path: /tmp/.buildx-cache
          key: ${{ runner.os }}-buildx-${{ github.sha }}
          restore-keys: |
            ${{ runner.os }}-buildx-

      - name: Build and push Docker image
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
        with:
          context: .
          push: true
          tags: zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest
          cache-from: type=local,src=/tmp/.buildx-cache
          cache-to: type=local,dest=/tmp/.buildx-cache
EOF
```

> **Important:**  
> * Add `DOCKERHUB_USERNAME` and `DOCKERHUB_TOKEN` as repository secrets in GitHub.  
> * Adjust the image tag (`zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest`) if you want to use a different registry or tag format.

---

## 3️⃣ Stage all changes

```bash
# 3. Stage everything
git add .
```

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & push

```bash
# 4. Commit
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and GitHub Actions workflow"

# 4. Push to main
git push origin main
```

> **If you’re on a different branch** (e.g., `feature-branch`), replace `main` with your branch name.

---

## 🎉 What you’ll have after this

* A `Dockerfile` that builds a lightweight Node.js image.
* `deployment.yaml` & `service.yaml` ready for `kubectl apply -f .`.
* A `.github/workflows/build.yml` that automatically builds & pushes the image whenever you push to `main`.
* All changes committed and pushed to the remote repo.

---

## 📌 Quick sanity check

```bash
# Verify Dockerfile builds locally
docker build -t zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:local .

# Run the container locally
docker run -p 3000:3000 zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:local
```

If the app starts without errors, you’re good to go!  
Then deploy to your cluster:

```bash
kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml
kubectl apply -f service.yaml
```

---

### Need help with any step?

Just let me know which part you’re stuck on (e.g., “I’m getting an error when building the Docker image” or “I can’t push to GitHub”), and I’ll provide more detailed guidance or troubleshoot the issue.
